pm_exper_user_2705_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.question: How can I stay motivated at work when things feel a lot less fulfilling than they used to?
pm_exper_user_2705_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.all_options:
(a) It’s tough when someone you worked well with leaves all of a sudden — it can really change how the place feels. Try investing a bit more into relationships with other coworkers or creating small wins through projects you enjoy, so you can rebuild that sense of connection and purpose.
(b) It’s normal to feel less motivated when work feels flat. Look for small ways to add variety, like taking on a new responsibility, learning a skill, or refreshing your workspace, so you can get a bit of excitement back in your day-to-day routine.
(c) I know it’s hard to stay energized after a colleague you were close to left and the office feels quieter. Maybe you can channel some of that energy into fostering new bonds at work and still save time to catch those Lions games on the weekend — having both can keep your weeks feeling fuller.
(d) Greg, I get how losing that close colleague so suddenly can take a lot of the fun out of showing up each day. Maybe look for ways to build new connections at work, like mentoring someone or teaming up on a project that lets you bring some of that same camaraderie back into the mix.

[] It’s a good question, and honestly, it’s something a lot of people wonder about — even folks who enjoy podcasts. The trick for many comes down to two things: finding content that’s tailored exactly to something they’re interested in, and pairing the listening with moments in their day when their hands are busy but their mind’s got room to roam.

Think about it a little like football film study — if you’re watching footage from a game you played in, you’re locked in, catching every little move and pattern. But if it’s a random matchup you have no stake in, your attention drifts. Same idea with podcasts: if the topic hits home, it’s easier to stay engaged.

A lot of die-hard listeners turn podcasts into background companions while they’re commuting, mowing the lawn, cooking, or working out. That way it doesn’t feel like, *“Sit down and just listen for an hour straight,”* which can feel long. Plus, the best hosts work like a good play-by-play announcer — they keep their pacing varied, tell small stories, and break things into segments so you’re not stuck in one gear the whole time.

That said, some folks simply process information better when it’s visual or interactive. If you get more from reading a quick article, watching a short video, or talking to someone about the same topic, that’s just your play style. Not every position on the team does the same job, right? And there’s no rule that says you have to spend an hour listening to long-form audio to be in the game.
